Early planning and procurement have been essential as demand is high globally for HVDC cable and the specialised ships needed to install it.

Only two global manufacturers still make the kind of HVDC cable we need in New Zealand. Getting them interested in a small project halfway around the world had its challenges, Noble says, but the challenge and pedigree of the Cook Strait link has its own appeal.

“We’re a very small country in a very remote place with a very small and complex scope of work. However, we are seen as iconic,” Noble says.

New Zealand's infrastructure challenges are complex, and no single organisation has all the answers. That's why sharing real-world experiences matters. Our aim with our ‘Infrastructure lessons from around New Zealand’ series is to spark new ideas and support better infrastructure planning, investment, and asset management across the country.

Read this case study: https://lnkd.in/eYdSve3V

Our Te Waihanga team presented research covering infrastructure costs, investment, productivity, housing, and decision-making.

On day one, Danny Kwon showcased a poster session on 'Institutional impact on infrastructure outcomes'. Lucy Groenhart, PhD. spoke about 'Economic analysis and infrastructure decision-making practice in New Zealand: Insights from 100 business cases'.

Day two featured an Infrastructure New Zealand Themed Session, chaired by Graham Campbell, featuring presentations from:

• Eliza Posthuma – 'Follow the money: What's driving infrastructure costs in New Zealand'
• Graham Campbell and Dr. Stuart Donovan – 'Forward Guidance modelling local and regional infrastructure supply'
• Talosaga Talosaga and Danny Kwon – 'Foundations for Growth: How Infrastructure Can Increase Productivity'.

Jiangheng Leo Lin gave a presentation featuring his PhD research, 'The Role of Wait Time Disclosures in Public Housing: Evidence from Seattle'.

We're proud to see our team contributing to discussions that help improve infrastructure decision-making in Aotearoa New Zealand.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/tewaihanga_earlier-this-month-te-waihanga-researchers-activity-7486246584406679552-r8xb"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"New Zealand Infrastructure Commission, Te Waihanga","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/tewaihanga"},"datePublished":"2026-07-22T04:14:14.517Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/tewaihanga_how-can-stronger-governance-help-new-zealand-activity-7485547734033285120-xxD-","text":"How can stronger governance help New Zealand deliver better infrastructure? 

That was the focus of our latest Infrastructure Leaders Network Meet-up, which brought senior public sector infrastructure leaders together at Parakiore Recreation and Sports Centre in Christchurch.

The meet-up explored the Government's response to the National Infrastructure Plan, the future direction of infrastructure assurance, and the role of project and organisational governance in supporting successful delivery.

Thank you to our speakers and panellists for sharing their insights and experience:

• Geoff Cooper, Te Waihanga
• Dr Kanchan Sharma (PhD), The Treasury - New Zealand
• Rebecca Robertshawe, Te Waihanga
• Dr Rod Carr, ASB Bank Board
• Raveen Jaduram and Sue Tindal, Te Waihanga Board

Participants also joined James Jowsey from Christchurch City Council and Cam McLean from Crown Infrastructure Delivery Ltd for a behind-the-scenes tour of Parakiore and a closer look at the delivery of this significant public infrastructure project.

New Zealand’s infrastructure challenges require capable leadership, clear governance, and opportunities for people across the system to learn from one another. The Infrastructure Leaders Network helps build those connections by bringing senior public sector leaders together to share practical experience and test ideas.

#Webinar #Infrastructure #TeWaihanga #Research","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/tewaihanga_webinar-infrastructure-tewaihanga-activity-7483383153823387649-KJCS"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"New Zealand Infrastructure Commission, Te Waihanga","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/tewaihanga"},"datePublished":"2026-07-13T03:10:30.715Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/tewaihanga_infrastructure-plan-tewaihanga-activity-7482270205034012672-1b1e","text":"💡PRIORITY SPOTLIGHT | In February we published our National Infrastructure Plan. In the Plan we’ve highlighted 10 priorities that New Zealand needs to focus on over the next decade. 
 
One of these priorities is to complete catch-up on renewals in the water sector and restore affordability – sector affordability can be restored through national guidance on demand management, resourcing the economic regulator and providing assurance over investment proposals. 
 
What’s the problem?

💧New Zealanders use more water and invest more in water-related infrastructure than almost any other high-income country. 
📈 Councils plan to spend close to $50 billion over the next decade on renewing and expanding water networks. 
💵 As a result, household bills are expected to double in some instances. 
📪 Sustaining current high levels of investment will be unaffordable for some communities. 
🏠 From mid-1970s to mid-1990s we spent less on water than the rate of depreciation – our pipes and treatment plants have worn out faster than we replaced them. 
🚿 Councils are now dealing with a legacy of broken pipes, sewage 
overflows and leaks, as well as a need to invest to meet quality standards set by Taumata Arowai. 
 
So, what do we need to do?

⚙️ Encourage councils and water services providers to consider installing water meters and adopting volumetric pricing. 
🏛️ Ensure regulatory coordination – the Commerce Commission, the Water Services Authority – Taumata Arowai and regional councils will need to work together.
 
Find out more here: https://lnkd.in/eG4r5-Sy

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Our team recently interviewed Roy Noble, HVDC Programme Director, at <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/transpower?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Transpower New Zealand</a> to explore how Transpower is planning the renewal of the Cook Strait high voltage direct current (HVDC) cables, which provide a crucial electricity connection between the North and South Islands.

Early planning and procurement have been essential as demand is high globally for HVDC cable and the specialised ships needed to install it.

Only two global manufacturers still make the kind of HVDC cable we need in New Zealand. Getting them interested in a small project halfway around the world had its challenges, Noble says, but the challenge and pedigree of the Cook Strait link has its own appeal.

“We’re a very small country in a very remote place with a very small and complex scope of work. However, we are seen as iconic,” Noble says.

New Zealand's infrastructure challenges are complex, and no single organisation has all the answers. That's why sharing real-world experiences matters. Our aim with our ‘Infrastructure lessons from around New Zealand’ series is to spark new ideas and support better infrastructure planning, investment, and asset management across the country.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="feed-reshare-content__commentary">In our next alumni profile, we would like you to meet <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/eliza-posthuma?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card_reshare-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card_reshare-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Eliza Posthuma</a>, a 2023 Bachelor of Commerce [BCom] graduate and Research Analyst at <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/tewaihanga?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card_reshare-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card_reshare-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>New Zealand Infrastructure Commission, Te Waihanga</a>.

She completed two more STAR courses the following semester before enrolling in the Bachelor of Commerce in 2021, initially studying Human Resource Management and minoring in Political Science. She later changed direction, graduating with a major in Economics and a minor in Statistics.
 
Eliza thought ECON104 was an amazing course and one that everyone should take because it helps us understand the world around us. She soon realised that she had an aptitude for Economics. It clicked for her, and she went on to enjoy every Economics course she took at UC.
 
After completing her degree in 2023, Eliza secured an Analytics and Research in Government (ARG) internship and was placed with the <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/ministry-of-business-innovation-and-employment?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card_reshare-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card_reshare-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment</a>. At the end of the internship, she started a full-time position as a Data Analyst in the Markets team. In that role, Eliza compiled, analysed and reported on energy-sector data. The position also involved considerable stakeholder engagement, which she enjoyed.
 
After two years at MBIE, Eliza moved to the Infrastructure Commission. When she joined around 10 months ago, the National Infrastructure Plan was about to be published. She has found it especially rewarding to see the government’s response to the Plan and the wide support the Plan has received. 

Eliza enjoys her work because it has the potential to have an impact, particularly with the opportunity to contribute to the evidence base for infrastructure in New Zealand. According to Eliza, Economics is highly valued at the Commission, so she has been able to put her UC studies to very good use. She also values her close-knit team. Her immediate team of five colleagues is made up of people she describes as exceptionally smart and hard-working, while also being highly approachable and genuinely lovely people.
 
Outside work, Eliza enjoys baking sourdough, crocheting, playing futsal and catching up with friends. We are particularly interested in the freshly baked sourdough and are already considering travel plans to sample it!
 
While at university, Eliza and a friend made a promise that they would take a major overseas trip after working for two years. Last summer, the time was up, and they kept their promise. Over six weeks, they travelled through eight countries: the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria, Italy, France, Scotland and Vatican City. That sounds like a wonderful trip and an excellent promise to make and keep.
 
Thank you so much for catching up with us, Eliza. We wish you all the best in your important work at the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission.

</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">🎤 | Earlier this month, Te Waihanga researchers shared their latest work on infrastructure economics at the New Zealand Association of Economists' 66th annual conference in Christchurch, which brings together local and international economists.

Day two featured an Infrastructure New Zealand Themed Session, chaired by <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/graham-campbell-4a83b83a?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Graham Campbell</a>, featuring presentations from:

• <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/eliza-posthuma?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Eliza Posthuma</a> – 'Follow the money: What's driving infrastructure costs in New Zealand'
• <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/graham-campbell-4a83b83a?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Graham Campbell</a> and Dr. Stuart Donovan – 'Forward Guidance modelling local and regional infrastructure supply'
• <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/talosaga-talosaga-5417aa27?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Talosaga Talosaga</a> and Danny Kwon – 'Foundations for Growth: How Infrastructure Can Increase Productivity'.

<a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/jiangheng-leo-lin-138564105?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Jiangheng Leo Lin</a> gave a presentation featuring his PhD research, 'The Role of Wait Time Disclosures in Public Housing: Evidence from Seattle'.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">How can stronger governance help New Zealand deliver better infrastructure? 

That was the focus of our latest Infrastructure Leaders Network Meet-up, which brought senior public sector infrastructure leaders together at Parakiore Recreation and Sports Centre in Christchurch.

The meet-up explored the Government's response to the National Infrastructure Plan, the future direction of infrastructure assurance, and the role of project and organisational governance in supporting successful delivery.

Thank you to our speakers and panellists for sharing their insights and experience:

• <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/geoffckcooper?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Geoff Cooper</a>, Te Waihanga
• Dr Kanchan Sharma (PhD), <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/new-zealand-treasury?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>The Treasury - New Zealand</a>
• Rebecca Robertshawe, Te Waihanga
• Dr Rod Carr, <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/asb-bank?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>ASB Bank</a> Board
• <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/raveen-jaduram-6453596?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Raveen Jaduram</a> and Sue Tindal, Te Waihanga Board

Participants also joined James Jowsey from <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/christchurch-city-council?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Christchurch City Council</a> and Cam McLean from <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/crowninfrastructuredelivery?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Crown Infrastructure Delivery Ltd</a> for a behind-the-scenes tour of Parakiore and a closer look at the delivery of this significant public infrastructure project.

New Zealand’s infrastructure challenges require capable leadership, clear governance, and opportunities for people across the system to learn from one another. The Infrastructure Leaders Network helps build those connections by bringing senior public sector leaders together to share practical experience and test ideas.

Thank you to everyone who took part and contributed to the discussion.</p>

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">💡PRIORITY SPOTLIGHT | In February we published our National Infrastructure Plan. In the Plan we’ve highlighted 10 priorities that New Zealand needs to focus on over the next decade. 
 
One of these priorities is to complete catch-up on renewals in the water sector and restore affordability – sector affordability can be restored through national guidance on demand management, resourcing the economic regulator and providing assurance over investment proposals. 
 
What’s the problem?

💧New Zealanders use more water and invest more in water-related infrastructure than almost any other high-income country. 
📈 Councils plan to spend close to $50 billion over the next decade on renewing and expanding water networks. 
💵 As a result, household bills are expected to double in some instances. 
📪 Sustaining current high levels of investment will be unaffordable for some communities. 
🏠 From mid-1970s to mid-1990s we spent less on water than the rate of depreciation – our pipes and treatment plants have worn out faster than we replaced them. 
🚿 Councils are now dealing with a legacy of broken pipes, sewage 
overflows and leaks, as well as a need to invest to meet quality standards set by Taumata Arowai. 
 
So, what do we need to do?

⚙️ Encourage councils and water services providers to consider installing water meters and adopting volumetric pricing. 
🏛️ Ensure regulatory coordination – the Commerce Commission, the Water Services Authority – Taumata Arowai and regional councils will need to work together.
